utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Please be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth, the interpreters, the Registry, counsel for the Prosecution, counsel for the Defence. Before beginning, I should like to give the floor to Mr. Jovan Simic. There seems to be a problem with Mr. Prcac. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, we do have a problem. Mr. Prcac fell ill yesterday. As you can see, he is absent from the courtroom. May I explain briefly what happened. He felt very unwell but he wasn't taken to hospital immediately. They had to wait until the Krnojelac trial ended. Then he was taken to the Tribunal, kept in the garage for about 15 minutes and then transferred to the hospital, where he stayed until about 10.00 p.m., upon which he was returned to the Detention Unit, advised to rest and go to sleep. I must note with great regret that the ruling of this Trial Chamber is not being respected. We have discussed this matter repeatedly. You have given certain recommendations regarding this problem. Ms. Brenda Hollis, the former Prosecutor, agreed that she had nothing against Mr. Prcac enjoying the same treatment as all the other detainees, but for some reasons which we are unaware of, this did not happen. We did write a letter to the Registry and to the President of this Tribunal, Mr. Jorda. We received no reply so we don't know what's happening. So this seems to be a vicious circle. Mr. Prcac is an elderly man; he is a sick man. He cannot endure the treatment he's being given. I really don't know who to blame, but this kind of treatment is certainly worsening his medical condition. We have two problems here. First of all, we cannot prepare for the Defence properly with our defendant being ill; and secondly, if this continues, we shall have to suspend the continuation of the hearings. As for today, we agree that we continue with the hearings, but the plan of this team had been for Mr. Prcac to hear the cross-examination of Mr. Radic, and unless his condition improves, I will not be able to agree that the cross-examination of Mr. Radic be conducted in the absence of Mr. Prcac. I appeal to Your Honours once again, because I don't understand why four defendants can walk around, can talk, can enjoy recreation together, whereas Mr. Prcac cannot; that they can be transported together, whereas Mr. Prcac has to wait two hours for the transport. He has high blood pressure. He is a man who suffers from various ailments. And out of professional ethics, I have to caution this Trial Chamber that we are heading in a direction that could have tragic consequences. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the first that I have heard of today, and I would like to express also the concern of the Prosecution if, in fact, there was a delay in medical attention being rendered to Mr. Prcac. This is irrespective of anything Ms. Hollis may have said. If what Mr. Simic is indicating is the state of affairs, I think that this could have some consequences that we are very concerned about as well. I would like to join in the concern and ask, perhaps, the Chamber to look into what the delay was in rendering the assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you very much for your concern, Ms. Susan Somers. But perhaps you could look into the matter in the Office of the Prosecutor, because, as Mr. Jovan Simic has mentioned, we did raise the question here in the courtroom. I see that Judge Wald has a comment to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My only comment was that this did come up in your predecessors, and in fact originally there was some question whether the Prosecutor, originally, way back, had requested some kind of special transportation arrangements for Mr. Prcac. But then they retreated. My memory is that they retreated from that and agreed that he could be treated like the others. So I tend to think it's in the Registry's lap.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I completely agree, but my concern --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: As long as you have already voiced very clearly here in front of both of the counsel and us that to your knowledge you have no objection to him being treated similarly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We have no objection to assisting him physically as he needs it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. That was exactly what I was going to say to Ms. Susan Somers. There was at least one contradiction. Ms. Susan Somers said that in this courtroom, and for the transcript, that they had nothing against Mr. Prcac being transported together with the other accused. The problem is that the Prosecutor requested a restriction of communication, and as a result of those restrictions, all these problems arose. I know that the Registry asked the Prosecutor in writing whether, yes or no, restrictions were needed, and the Office of the Prosecutor officially confirmed that, yes, they needed these restrictions. So we have one position of the Prosecutor here in the courtroom and another position of the Prosecutor outside the courtroom. I think that is the problem. I know, Mr. Jovan Simic, and I personally in the next break will address the matter. I know that the President is informed of the issue, we have already discussed it, and during the next break, I am going to speak personally with the President and I'm going to ask the Registry - maybe I should wait for Madam Registrar, for her to finish her conversation - I'm going to ask the Registry to convey to the President of the Tribunal this part of the transcript in which Mr. Jovan Simic stated what he did, the position expressed by Ms. Susan Somers, and the entire discussion that we have had so that the President may be in a position to take a decision as quickly as possible. That is as much as I can do. As you know, it is not up to the Chamber to decide about such matters. It is up to the President. As you know, the President was seized of the matter a few weeks ago, and I think that we need to have a decision very quickly. Ms. Susan Somers, do you have something to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If the Court will permit me. Mr. Saxon informed me that apparently Ms. Hollis, having been informed of the medical problems, had on the record - and I would try to locate it perhaps on the break - indicated that the position had in fact changed, and I certainly adhere to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not only for gentlemanly reasons that I'm trying to defend Ms. Hollis. She's not here so that's only fair. Ms. Hollis' position was clear, that all five defendants need to have the same treatment, and that is the problem. If you remember, she requested the same measures for all five and she couldn't understand why it was being applied to Prcac and not to the other accused. That was her position. After that, she agreed that all of them should have equal treatment. I apologise for intervening at this stage with this comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. So our conclusion is that we must decide the matter as urgently as possible. That is what we are able to do. So I insist that the Registry convey to the President an abstract of the transcript regarding this matter so he can have more information at his disposal. I also need to tell Mr. Stojanovic the dates designated for the Defence of the accused Mr. Zigic. So it is -- I'm talking of the week, the week of the 26th of March, the week of the 9th of April, the week of the 17th of April - I must say that these two weeks are a little shorter, as you know, because there are holidays in between - and the week of the 23rd of April, which means that we will stick to the plan we announced for the week of the 7th of May for the Defence of Mr. Prcac, and also the week of the 14th of May for Mr. Prcac. That is what we plan and that is what we will abide by for the moment. I think that we are now able to begin with our work proper, and for that purpose, I give the floor to Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence calls Witness Vinka Andzic, and we have five witnesses planned for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Vinka Andzic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are going to read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Please make yourself as comfortable as possible. Thank you very much for coming. First you will be answering questions put to you by Mr. Fila. Wait a moment, please, because I see there is a problem with one of the court reporters. I think that we can now proceed. Mr. Fila, you have the floor. Examined by Mr. Fila:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Vinka Andzic, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of August, 1959.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: In Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by ethnicity, you are what?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry for interrupting, but I'm concerned, looking at the transcript, that the witness has not taken the oath. I just wanted to check on that. That's all. THE COURT REPORTER: It's there but it didn't appear on the transcript because my computer was frozen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you satisfied now? The English court reporter tells us that it is not in the transcript but it will be entered. It is in the memory and it will be entered subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm satisfied. Thank you, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any event, your remark has been registered in the record. So, Mr. Fila, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity and religion?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your occupation?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: A dressmaker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the conflict began, where did you work and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I worked in the Omarska mine as a cleaning lady.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married? Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I am married. I have a husband and two sons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the building in which you work the same building in which people would later be detained?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were working before that event, did you use the water in the mine, and how?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, we used the water normally, at the tap, industrial water that we all used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it water running from the taps?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did that water come from, from a well or from the town water supply system?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: From a well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on when this investigation centre was established, and after that too, was that same water used?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you a few questions about a person called Mladjo Radic. Did you know him before the war, and how?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him as a quiet, nice man, a nice policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when the investigations centre was established in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I think it was at the beginning of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who worked with you in the hygiene maintenance?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: My colleague, Bosana Nisevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you work? What were your working hours?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: From 7.00 a.m. until 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What exactly did you clean?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: We cleaned the upstairs floor where the inspectors were; also downstairs we cleaned a couple of times. And then the detainees themselves told us that it was not necessary, that they would do it, that we just give them the products to clean with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the existence of the centre, did you see Mladjo Radic? If you did, where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I saw him in an office. In front of that office there was a corridor and the steps, and there was an archway, and he would patrol in that area, he would walk around in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he doing on that staircase?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Nothing. He just walked around there. That was probably his assignment, to work there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know what kind of weapon he had at the time when you saw him there?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: He had an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in an office as well, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In that particular office, he would sit there occasionally, answer the phone, and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your colleague and yourself cleaned all those premises?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those premises, would you come across traces of blood?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, a little, occasionally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there rooms in which people worked, and who?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, the inspectors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sometimes hear screams and moans?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sometimes see any one of the detainees being hit?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, occasionally, but not very often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any women on that floor?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were some women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there several of them?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly how many. Not many but there were some.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they clean those rooms as well?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, they cleaned their own rooms, but sometimes they helped us as well because they were bored.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they spend the night?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: They had two offices on the upper floor where they spent the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the day, where were they?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: In the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have freedom to move around the building?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did they move?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: They could walk around. Not exactly anywhere they wanted, but they could go outside, they could walk along the corridor, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they able to use the bathroom?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did use the bathroom. Everything was okay. They had showers and everything. They washed their own clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they, perhaps, use a hotplate to cook on?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, to make coffee or tea or to prepare some food for themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that hotplate?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: They had one, and there was another one in the office in which Mr. Radic was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the largest room on that floor? And if you do, what was it called?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a hall, like a conference room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the day when the investigators were there --

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- were the guards there also and the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that there were a lot of people on that floor at the time?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were a certain number of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all the rooms occupied then?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in touch with all those women?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any one of them complain to you about Mladjo Radic's behaviour?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: No, no, on the contrary. They praised him. They said that he was a fine man, that he treated them correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you perhaps give us the names of some women who told you that?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: There was [redacted] who said that, [redacted], I think that was her name, Jadranka Cigelj, and another woman who worked in the Red Roses Cafe. Several of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person, [redacted], did she have another name as well?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I think she had another surname, [redacted], something like that. I can't remember. But she worked with me for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally see Mladjo Radic bring things to the women detainees?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he bring them?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: He brought them food, tins of food, bread, hygiene products, whatever they asked for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did one of them celebrate her birthday?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was Cigelj or the other one, but I know that one of them did celebrate her birthday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question for you now. Please let us focus on the lady called [redacted]. Did it ever occur that Mladjo Radic sent you to fetch her and you took her upstairs to this big room that you called a conference room where Mladjo Radic was alone during the day, and then he raped her?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last question. How would you describe Mladjo Radic's behaviour towards the women and the other detainees, as far as you were able to see?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: The behaviour of a nice man, a good man. I really don't know how to explain it in any other way. I think they should have been grateful to him for all he did for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The Defence has no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would any of the other Defence counsel like to ask questions of this witness? I see negative signs coming from them. No? The Prosecution, the cross-examination will be conducted by Mr. Saxon; is that right? Yes, Mr. Saxon, you have the floor. Mrs. Vinka Andzic, you will now be answering questions put to you by the Prosecutor. Your witness, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I begin the cross-examination, I would just like to inform the Trial Chamber of one thing. While I was cross-examining Mr. Radovan Medic yesterday, Judge Riad had some questions about Defence Exhibit D16/3, and there were questions about that exhibit vis-à-vis some pronouns and the English translation of those pronouns. And I simply wanted to inform the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution is resubmitting this document to the Translation Unit to see if there are errors in the translation. Cross-examined by Mr. Saxon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Andzic, you mentioned in your direct testimony that you used the water normally at the tap, "industrial water that we all used." That was your testimony. Were you using the same water that was used for the mining processes at the camp, the processing of iron ore and things like that, or were you using a different water system?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: We used the same water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that you drank that water?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The corridor, you talked about the large conference room that was at the end of the corridor on the first floor of the administration building; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fila asked you a question as to whether you had ever brought this woman with the last name of [redacted] to that conference room, and then whether Mr. Radic had then raped her in that conference room, and your answer was no.

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question for you is: Did Mr. Radic, at any time, ask you to bring -- before I finish my question, Your Honour, may we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let us move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in public session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Andzic, you knew some of the people detained at the Omarska camp during that summer of 1992, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of the detainees who you knew were killed at the Omarska camp; is that right? I remind you that you're under oath.

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps they were. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you know if any of the people that you knew were killed at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I couldn't see that. How could I see that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you saw --

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I couldn't walk around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You couldn't walk around. Why not?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Well, because I had no time. I was always busy working upstairs, on the floor above.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spent 12 hours straight, from 7.00 in the morning until 7.00 in the evening, cleaning that first floor, when you just told us that the female detainees there told you that after awhile they could clean it themselves? We haven't heard an answer.

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I went to the Separacija for a time too, and we would do some work there and then come back and do some work here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left the administration building, did you see people being mistreated at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I would see someone slap someone sometimes, things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned before that you heard the sounds of screams, moans from the first floor, when you were working on the first floor of the administration building. You said that occasionally you saw detainees being hit. Did you report these incidents or did you just become used to it and then ignore it?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I didn't become used to it. Quite simply, I did my work. I couldn't ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You couldn't what? Would you finish the thought, please?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I couldn't watch it. I was doing my job, going about my business; they were doing their job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had children at the time, didn't you, Mrs. Andzic, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. One of my sons -- one son was -- well, I don't remember how old I was or he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Andzic, it was painful for you to watch the mistreatment of those prisoners, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: As I said, I didn't watch it. I went about my own business. It wasn't up to me to watch it. But if they were slapped or something, that ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you finished your work for the day at the Omarska camp, after spending those 12-hour days there, did you talk to anyone about what you saw at the camp, the mistreatment of prisoners, seeing prisoners slapped, hearing moans?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Well, no, they just asked me whether they had enough food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see mistreatment -- I'll rephrase that. You said that the women could walk around freely and you said that they could go outside. What did you mean by the term "outside"?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: To go outside in the meadow, to pick the various plants there and show us what teas could be made from which plants, and that's what we would do. We would pick the flowers and plants and make the tea and drink it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to us where exactly this meadow was with these plants that you used to make tea?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Roundabout the buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Roundabout which buildings?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Around the administration building, the workshop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I'm just trying to understand you. There was a meadow around the administration building and around the workshop. By "the workshop," do you mean the building that was also called the hangar?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How big was this meadow?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Enormous. Those meadows are enormous, enormous. There's nothing there, just that part, and there's a petrol pump and the "white house."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there cows grazing on this meadow that was around the hangar and the administration building?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I understand you correctly, you're saying that the female detainees would walk out of the administration building and walk on this meadow and pick plants; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever go with them and ask to see the kind of plants that they were picking? Were you interested in that?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was very interested in those plants, and I use those same plants still, today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you go with to pick plants off of that meadow?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: With the women. They didn't all go. Several of them went. I don't actually know their names but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall the names of the women who went with you, any names?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember. A lot of time has gone by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were outside the administration building, going out to that meadow or meadows, did you see any detainees outside the administration building?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were in front, in front of the administration building. Between the building and the hangar, that's where they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any guards out there?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the prisoners look who were out there, that you saw?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to describe their appearance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you try?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, some of them were standing; some of them were sitting down; some of them were silent; some of them would smile, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the camp smell when you were outside the administration building?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Well, it was an unpleasant smell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "unpleasant"?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to explain it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did it smell of? What were you smelling?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember, but all I know is it wasn't a fresh smell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: A strange smell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the male detainees go with you and the female detainees out to the meadow to pick plants?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could I have the Trial Chamber's indulgence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Fila, any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to clarify matters. Re-examined by Mr. Fila:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a question about the water, whether the water went through the taps and was then -- went into the glasses and drunk, before the investigations centre was set up, during its duration and afterwards.

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: We drank the water from the taps. We poured it into glasses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is my first question. My second question: Could the witness, on the model - I don't know why the model has been removed - but could she indicate where the meadows were, the place where she saw Mladjo Radic on guard? If the Chamber so permits.

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I can show it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you think that is necessary, Mr. Fila, to have the model put up in front of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't think it is at all necessary, but just in view of the questions that Mr. Saxon has just asked. Otherwise, I don't think it's necessary. But she can get up and point to what she was describing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That would mean that we all have to rise. Mr. Usher, would it be possible to set up the model in front of the witness again, if you have somebody to help you perhaps? Would that be at all possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could solve this question with a photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well. We can place the photo on the ELMO. Do you have a photo, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number is Prosecution Exhibit 3/34. Prosecution Exhibit 3/34.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I'm just trying to clarify things. The exhibit that Mr. Fila has referred to shows the Keraterm camp, so I think we need to look at a different exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. In the list of documents, it says the photograph of the Omarska camp, and that's the number that stands next to that particular exhibit, according to the list that we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, could you help us, please? Is there a photograph of the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will take me a few seconds to locate it because I need a number. Otherwise, I have to check it manually.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. D26/1 is the entrance to the administration building. 3/121, it says panorama of the Omarska camp. So the number is now 3/121. Or, Mr. President, I am told that the number is D30/1. D30/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vinka, take a look at this photograph, please, and indicate where the meadows that you talked about are located.

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: This here, here, over here. We passed around here. Roundabout, all the way around. That's the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, the transcript says "here." "Here" is not a very precise location so perhaps we ought to define it better, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, take a look at the photograph and describe exactly where the meadows are, saying behind what, in front of what.

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: This is the hangar. This is the administration building. This is the field, pitch, playing ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are the meadows around the hangar and the "white house," the pista, opposite the pista; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On both sides of the hangar, a little further off; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And behind the administration building?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you -- did you go flower picking on all those meadows?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I apologise for that extra time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mrs. Andzic, good morning. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would like to understand something more in your testimony, which I followed very carefully. You are Serb. Were you detained in the Omarska camp or were you hired to clean or did you volunteer to clean? What was exactly your position?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I worked there. It was my duty to work there, to do that job, regardless of whether I'm a Serb or not. I never looked at what people's nationalities were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That's not my question. Were you detained or were you a worker?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: A worker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You were a worker. And you lived separately from the other women.

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You were living in a separate part from the other women, or were you all the time with them and seeing how they eat, how they feel, how they sleep?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Well, I could see it some of the time, not all of the time. When I had time, I would chat to them and then go about my business. Sometimes they would come up to me to help me wash the windows, for example. We would hang the curtains up and so on when we clean them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, let us see how -- what was your relationship exactly with Mr. Radic? Were you good friends or just you saw him here and there?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I would see him around. I knew him since my childhood as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. Were your family relations? Were you acquainted to know his character and so on?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You saw him sometimes in the office, sitting and answering the telephone. Was this possible for anybody, any guard, to sit in the office and answer the telephone, or only a few people who could sit in the office and answer the telephone?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, they could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Anybody could sit and answer the telephone?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: They could, yes, anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Any guard?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Anybody could, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So this office wasn't the office of the management or anybody. Just a public office.

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was also the investigation done in this office?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The blood you saw sometimes on the walls. Was it also in this office?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now you mentioned that his behaviour to the ladies or to the detained women, he was a nice man. What did you mean by that? Was he too nice to them? Was he all the time with them, trying to be nice to them?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: He was nice to everybody, to the men, to the women. His conduct was proper and he helped anybody he could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned that you did not lead this lady, [redacted] [redacted], to the conference room to see him. As you have been around all the time, were there any other -- did [redacted] go to him by her ownself, or what?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. No, she didn't go, nor would he allow himself something like that. Nobody sent me off, and I don't think any person would allow himself that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You spoke of the celebration of a birthday of Jadranka Cigelj and you mentioned in your statement that the guards brought drinks, cigarettes, and coffee.

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Who were these guards? Were they the shifts of Mr. Radic? Were they the guards working under him?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I can't remember who they were because a lot of time has gone by since then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. But who arranged that? Who asked these guards to bring the cigarettes and so on?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Themselves, probably themselves. When it was somebody's birthday, we would make a sort of collection and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So that was not related only to Mr. Radic. It was the custom in the camp that they celebrate the birthday of the detainees and bring them cigarettes and drinks?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That was?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Ms. Andzic, if I understand your testimony, you worked during the day in the centre, from 0700 to 1900 hours, and then you went home every night; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So you were not at the camp at any point during the night, during the time from --

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: -- until the next morning. Okay. You also said that at various times you saw Mr. Radic on the staircase doing guard duty or patrolling, and you also saw him sitting in the office where the telephones were. You also told us that you, in the building, while doing your cleaning, on occasion, on occasion, would hear screams or moans, and on occasion would see detainees being slapped around. Now, would somebody who was standing on guard where you saw Mr. Radic standing guard, or sitting in the room with the telephones where you saw him sitting, would they also be in a position to hear the screams and moans when they occurred or to see people being slapped around when that happened?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you, the last bit of what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Let me try again. When you said that you sometimes, occasionally, would hear screams or moans and, occasionally, would see detainees being slapped by the guards, would somebody who was standing in the staircase where you told us you saw Mr. Radic sometimes, or sitting in the room --

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: -- would they be in a position to hear those screams and moans or see those detainees being slapped around?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I think they could, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. That's all I wanted to know. Now, you also told us that you never heard any of the women detainees complain about Mr. Radic; rather, you heard them say nice things about him. Did you, in your excursions with the women --

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did you, in your excursions into the meadows with the women, or in your talking to them around the building, did you ever hear any of the women complain about any of the guards or anybody who mistreated them?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: No, no, not one single time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you -- you told us about Mr. Radic bringing food and toiletries, or that the women told you that he brought food and toiletries to them. In your observations, or from what you heard from the women themselves, was it your impression that Mr. Radic did spend time during the day talking to them, chatting with the women, in other words, that he was with them in a friendly way; or his only contact with him was when he actually brought this food and toiletries to them? From your own observations or from what you heard.

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Only when he brought them food, then I would see him. Afterwards, no, that they would chat and be friends, no, I couldn't notice that. He would just give them food and the toiletries and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My last question is: When you went on these plant excursions into the meadows, could you keep walking as far into the meadows as you wished, or were there some kind of soldiers on guard a distance away from the meadow beyond which detainees couldn't go?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that did exist. We couldn't go wherever we wanted to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Judge Wald. Mrs. Vinka Andzic, I have a few questions for you myself. Did you receive a salary for your work?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, did you have any obligation to work?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Normally, what was the subject of conversation that you had with the women? If you chatted to the women, what did you usually chat about, talk about?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I knew [redacted] because she worked with me for a long time, 10, perhaps 12 years. We worked together so we would talk about everything, about our families, about everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, did the women complain about being detained in front of you? Did they complain to you about that?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: They just asked me, "Why has all this happened? What's all this about?" and I would say, "Well, I'm asking myself the same question," that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you ever speak about the conditions that prevailed in the detention centre?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: The conditions? They had excellent conditions. They had food, they had somewhere to sleep, they had a bathroom, a shower. They were able to wash their clothes. Mladjo would bring them everything they needed. I would bring things for them from my own house. I would bring everybody things, as far as I was able. That's what we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you gain the impression that they were happy to be there?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Well, no, of course not. They weren't happy to be there. You can't be happy if you're detained. You don't have your freedom, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did they complain about anything to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Very well, Mrs. Andzic. I see that Judge Riad has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Andzic, you just mentioned to the President that you have the duty to work in the detention centre. What kind of duty was that? Was it a moral duty? Was it a national obligation? What was this duty? Were all women obliged to go and work there?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So what was it?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: No. I worked and, quite normally, I continued the work that I had been doing previously; I did the same work, the same job when they called me to continue doing the job I had always done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Before the detention centre, you were working there as a cleaning lady?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same thing, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Because you said in the beginning that you were a dressmaker.

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't do that work. You had to take the job that was available. So I was a cleaning woman since 1985, and I'm still a cleaning woman today. I've always been a cleaning lady.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you were a cleaning lady, and when it was changed into a detention centre, you continued working. Did they force you to work or you stayed of your own free will?

utterances.speaker: VINKA ANDZIC
utterances.text: I went on doing the same work, yes. I had to. It was my job; it was my duty, just the same as if, you know, whatever job you have, whatever employ. It was my duty to go to work. Nobody forced me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Vinka Andzic, we have no further questions to ask you. We thank you very much for coming and we wish you a safe journey back to your place of residence. I'm now going to ask the usher to accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are calling our next witness, Borka Vrhovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mrs. Vrhovac. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will now read the solemn declaration which the usher will give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Thank you for coming to testify. Now you will be answering questions that Mr. Fila, who is to your left, will ask of you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Fila:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vrhovac, where and when were you born?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: I was born near Prijedor on the 13th of February, 1949.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your religion?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: I am married and a mother of two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What education do you have?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Secondary agricultural school and high teaching school in Zemun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you live? Where do you work?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: I live in Omarska, and I work for Polje Promet Omarska which is an agricultural cooperative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know the Radic family, specifically Mladjo Radic, and since when?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: I knew the Radics because they were our neighbours. We lived in the same building. It was a very nice family. I never heard anything bad about them. We socialised because we were neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Same building. What town?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: In Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then when he left Omarska and moved over to Prijedor, did you meet again?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Well, at times, yes, we'd meet. If I would go to Prijedor, yes, we would meet on occasion. Not particularly often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that at some point an investigations centre or a camp, as some call it, was formed in the Omarska mine?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of the investigations centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sometime in the middle of the year?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: In May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or maybe June?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mladjo Radic call you in relation to that investigations centre? What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Mr. Radic brought me a letter written by a lady in the investigations centre, asking me to send her clothes. I knew her from the -- because I was the president of the women's organisation in Omarska and that is how I knew her. So she sent me this letter, she signed it, and was asking me for some clothes. And I took those clothes to Mr. Radic to hand those clothes over to her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I don't see well. Did you tell us the name of that person? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was she employed somewhere?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the first time you learned that she was in that investigations centre?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you prepared those clothes to send to her, you gave it to Mladjo Radic, as you told us?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: I took it to his flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: That he would do it on different occasions because it was difficult for him to take it in one go, because I had taken a few changes of clothes. And he said that he would try to give it to her in installments, as it were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But why couldn't he take it all at once? Why was that? Was there something wrong about that?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Well, those were the times. People were saying that there was some kind of ethnic war, that there was intolerance of sorts, and he thought that it would be best if he didn't do it all at once, because it was said that there were people who were the enemies of our people and ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it wasn't -- it couldn't really be good if he were seen in public carrying those things, would it?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also send something to some other detainees?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I don't know their names. But be that as it may, all the women knew my name because I was the chairman of the women's organisation and that is how we cooperated. So if somebody knew somebody, he would or she would give my name and I sent things to various people through those who were on duty in the investigations centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not do it only through Mladjo Radic, did you?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: No, not only. I also sent things through other people who worked for the police or had connections with the police. I remember twins, one of the twins. My colleague sent a note to me asking me to send some food, some bread, and the young person -- there were young persons involved and I thought they would need more of them. Afterwards I met them in Prijedor and their mother, and I know that they are somewhere in Holland but I don't know what they are doing. I haven't heard about them since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they received what you sent them.

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, they did, and they thanked me. The sister's name was Azra and she worked in the post office in Kozarac, and I met her in Prijedor when I went -- as I was on my way to the bank. She was thanking me and saying that she would never forget it. But then I heard that they had left to the Netherlands, and I did not hear from them again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last question: During your acquaintanceship with the Radic family, and especially Mladjo Radic, did you ever notice any signs of ethnic intolerance towards other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: No, never. They were -- they are a very nice family. I never noticed anything of the sorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do other Defence counsel have any questions? No? I see they are indicating that they do not. Very well. Thank you. Now, Witness, you will answer the questions which the Prosecution will ask you. Yes, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Waidyaratne:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, Mrs. Vrhovac, where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: I work for the agricultural cooperative. That's where I was employed before the war, during the war, and where I still work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a representative of the firm Zepter?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your function in that organisation?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: I'm a Zepter associate. I'm their salesperson, and I sell, on their behalf, various cosmetics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vrhovac, what is the name of your husband?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Radivoje Vrhovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's his occupation?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: He is an agricultural technician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he mobilised during the conflict, the war?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: He was mostly under labour obligation in Poljopromet, because he was an -- he is an agricultural expert. He led the group that was responsible for the sewing and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vrhovac, you are a person who has been engaged in a women's association; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the president in 1992, January, in the women's organisation, [redacted]

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: In Omarska neighbourhood community, I was the chairman, the president of the women's organisation, and in the Kozarac neighbourhood community, it was Kadira Kahrimanovic. I do not know whether Sabiha was her deputy; I don't know that. But I cooperated with Mrs. Kadira Kahrimanovic who chaired the organisation in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vrhovac, were you a member of any other association during the conflict and after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Only the president of the women's organisation; nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of the Association of Serb Sisters during the war in Prijedor? Do you know that association?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: I know about that organisation but I wasn't a member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of the women's organisation of the 5th Kozarac Brigade, which was called in short form PET? I'm sure you remember that as you were the chairwoman.

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: I was the president of the women's organisation and thus I worked, cooperated, with women. We did simply what we had to do at the time, that is, preparing food, collecting clothes, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was whether you were the chairman -- chairwoman of the association of the 5th Kozarac Brigade which was called PET, during and after the war?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: I don't know of that name. I'm not aware of that name. Naturally, I worked for it because we collected woollen socks or we knit them. I organised women to knit woollen socks for the troops and we gathered food and carried it to them. I don't remember its name. Perhaps I misunderstood something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't understand your answer. You say, "I don't know that name," but then subsequently you say, "Naturally, I worked for it because we collected woollen socks." Did you organise an evening where woollen socks were knitted and were collected for the soldiers in the front, the Serbian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I organised it, that we knitted socks and collected food and carried it over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you visit the front and see to the soldiers who were in the front and the wounded, you and your organisation?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: I did go to take the food on Easter, and I took them eggs and sweets and woollen socks, woollen socks which were knit by the women in the organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went to the front and saw the soldiers and the wounded in the front; yes or no? That's what you said; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: I did see soldiers but not the wounded, because I only carried it to a certain place and turned it over. I never saw any wounded; I cannot say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vrhovac, you knew that there was a camp where your earlier friends, former friends, were detained in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to the camp and attend to those people at any time?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: I helped by sending food. I never went there, I never went there at all. But I said, I already said --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make a request to go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Mr. Waidyaratne allow the witness to finish the sentence and thus give the proper answer, to let the witness say what she has to say? Or perhaps Mr. Waidyaratne will answer for her.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: No, I won't -- I would allow the witness to speak, Your Honour. I'm sorry if I disturbed the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vrhovac, now you spoke about the instance where Mr. Radic informed you about a person Sabiha who was detained at the Omarska camp. What exactly did you send? What was the parcel that you gave to Mr. Radic to be taken to the camp?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: The letter said that she needed some warm clothes, and I know I sent some underwear with long sleeves, some T-shirts, and I remember a pair of yellow trousers made of Indian cotton. It was in summertime. But to remember every detail, really, I can't. I do know that there were some body warmers with long sleeves, and I remember those trousers made of Indian cotton.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the detention or thereafter, did you meet [redacted] at any time after her detention? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know as to whether she received all of what you are supposed to have sent through Mr. Radic? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at any time ask Mr. Radic as to why these people were detained?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Radic tell you as to why these people were detained?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: No, we did not discuss it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The time, Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Last question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your testimony in direct examination that, "These were people who were enemies of our people." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Well, simply that is -- I didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will Mr. Waidyaratne read what she said exactly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: That's what I did, Your Honour. I would even quote the line and the page if Mr. Fila wants it, but only thing, it's taking the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but let us spend time to cut -- or rather, the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waidyaratne, will you please check if the witness said because -- ask first the witness if she did, indeed, say that, and after that then proceed to asking your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say, "These were people who were enemies of our people," and, and you stopped. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waidyaratne, Mr. Waidyaratne, first one question and then the second. You cannot say -- wait for her answer. You cannot say, "Did you say that and what did you mean by it?" Wait for the answer to your first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say, "These were people who were enemies of our people"?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: When the investigations centre was set up, it was said that there were conflicts which -- the enemy of our people, and the investigations centre was set up to prove it or disprove it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. Mr. Fila, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is whether the witness is voicing her own opinion that they are the enemies of the Serb people, or whether it was said, whether it was rumoured that they were the enemies of the Serb people. That is what needs to be clarified because there is a difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila. Ask your question. Re-examined by Mr. Fila:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vrhovac, are you giving us your opinion, that they are the enemies of the Serb people, or is it that you said that when I asked you why couldn't all be taken at once, that it was too dangerous because it was said that they were the enemies of the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Correct, the latter. That is what was said, and that is why it was dangerous to take it all at once, and one could take food only in small quantities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was not your opinion, it was the story that went around.

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I testified to the story that went around during those days when the investigations centre was set up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't know who was there because you had never been to it.

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: I had never been to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know why people were there?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: No, I don't, not exactly. Because conflicts started. No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The next thing that I want to know, and to clarify this, you were the president of the women's organisation in the Omarska neighbourhood community; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was before the war?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then during the war, during all that, did you change the name of that women's organisation?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: That organisation went on working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you change it to some other name that Mr. Waidyaratne mentioned?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: I'm not -- no, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last question: Do you consider it an embarrassment, do you consider it a disgrace to collect things and to help people who are fighting against your people?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I did that because, no, I did not think it would disgrace me in any manner, and that is why I helped whoever asked me to help him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Fila. Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. I have just a very few. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: The women's organisation before the war that you were president of, you said that [redacted] had been a member of it and that's how you knew her when you got the letter asking for clothes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: [redacted] socialised with us because she was in the women's organisation in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right, I understand that. I wanted to clarify. Then the women's organisations before the war had both Serb and Muslim members? I mean, in other words, Muslim women could belong as well as Serb women, maybe Croat women; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, after the war broke out, you told us that the women's organisation continued to function during the war.

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did it continue to function with Muslim members, with Muslim women belonging? Did they continue -- did some Muslim women continue to be members of the women's organisation after the war started?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: There was a Croat woman who worked with us. Unfortunately, she passed away. And those women who happened to be there just went on working. Women who used to live and work in my organisation before that simply went on working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Including some Muslim women? In other words, during the war, did the women's organisation have any Muslim women working with it?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: That organisation had stopped working; that is, we were not active. The Omarska neighbourhood community organisation went on working as before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And did it have any Muslim members during the war, the Omarska neighbourhood women's community organisation?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, my only other question is, when I first heard you testify, and I want to make sure that this is correct - tell me if it's not correct - I thought that you said that when you brought the clothes for Mr. Radic to take to [redacted], there were a lot of clothes and that Mr. Radic said he might not be able to take them all at once because it might not look good if it were too obvious he was taking so many clothes because there were people that said people in the camp were enemies of the people; and that it was Mr. Radic who said there were others who believed that the people in the camp were enemies of the people, and that's why he wasn't going to take all the clothes at once. Is that right, or did I misunderstand?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: No, that is not what Mr. Radic said. Mr. Radic said, "I'll try to take it over on different occasions, to take it part by part."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So the business of some people thinking that people in the camp were enemies of the public was something you had heard other people say; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Wald. Mrs. Vrhovac, I also have two short questions. At the time, did you have an opinion about why some people were detained in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You could offer no reason at all?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: No, because I cooperated, I communicated, I had contact with my colleagues from the women's organisation until the very last moment. I simply didn't ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you tell us that you did not know what the reason was, that those people were the enemy of your people, that was that. But I wonder, and that is my question, did you have any idea, did you have any idea why were those people kept there?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you didn't know it; you never thought about that. Very well. Another question: In Omarska before the war, were there any Muslim women in your organisation?

utterances.speaker: BORKA VRHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
