utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Right, Mrs. Vrhovac, we do not have any further questions to ask you. Thank you very much for coming. We wish you successful work and a happy return to your home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The usher will help you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. We shall now make a break, a half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. I take advantage of this opportunity to inform the parties, and more specifically Mr. Jovan Simic, that I have indeed contacted the Office of the President and requested an urgent provisional decision, without prejudice, as to subsequent developments. So what I have promised I have done. We can now have the witness brought in, Mr. Fila, the next witness. Miroslav Rosic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is Miroslav Rosic, and Mr. Jovanovic will be the examiner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Miroslav Rosic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. [In English] Will you put on the other mic, please. Turn it on. Okay. [Interpretation] Thank you very much for coming. You will be first answering questions put to you by Mr. Jovanovic. Mr. Jovanovic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Jovanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, tell us, please, when you were born.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd of September, 1962.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where? Where were you born, Mr. Rosic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: In Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where are you living now?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: In Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you do?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: I drive an ambulance in the health centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, before the outbreak of the war in Prijedor, did you know Mladjo Radic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He was a policeman in Omarska and we lived close by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, can you think back to 1992, the end of May or the beginning of June, when you had to make a trip with your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Something linked to Mladjo Radic, in a way.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us about that event, and exactly what happened?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: Sometime at the end of May or the beginning of June, I don't know exactly, I know that I was on duty in the health centre, as usual, and there was a call from the police station; that is, Mr. Mladjo himself called up and said that a vehicle -- an ambulance was out of order on the road with a mother inside with a seriously injured child, and that we needed to go there immediately to transport the mother and child to the hospital in Banja Luka. And on that occasion, Mr. Radic mentioned that he had a family relationship with the mother and child in the car, and he asked me to assist them as much as I can and to stay with them for as long as is necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of the mother and the hurt boy?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: The lady's name was Senada, I think, Denic, and a nine- or eight-year-old boy whose name I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what ethnicity they were?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims. I think they were Muslims, judging by their names and surnames.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know whether they were linked to the Radic family?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mladjo mentioned that they were related. But as we set off very soon, then the child's mother, Mrs. Denic, told me that they were kums, that the two families had this kum relationship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were driving the ambulance in those days, did you go to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes. That evening too we stayed until late, and on the way back again, when I came home, Mladjo was waiting for me in the morning. He inquired about the condition of the mother and child and asked me to call him back and report to him on their improvement, whenever I had any contact with them, whenever I went to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take anything to Mrs. Denic and her son when you went to see them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: On the second day, Mladjo gave me some money. I think it was his salary that he just received. And he gave this money to me to give to her so that she would have it on her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take anything else, apart from money?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: On one occasion, that is, on the third or further day, I went to Banja Luka, I carried a parcel with food inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, are you aware of any of your colleagues or somebody else taking things to that family?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, the other drivers too were contacted by Mladjo and he sent food through them also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Mrs. Senada Denic tell you, if anything, when you met her, bringing her these things?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: The first day, the woman was terribly shaken up, as anyone would be because of the condition of the child. As I stayed there all night, whenever I would bring food or money, she would express endless gratitude to this person, to this man who had shown such concern for the child and herself. She was grateful to us as well but especially to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Rosic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any of the other Defence counsel that have any questions for this witness? I see they do not. In that case, Mr. Waidyaratne, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Waidyaratne:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, are you a relation of Mr. Zeljko Meakic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: He is a distant relative of my mother's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you live in the same flat where Mr. Meakic lives?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you live, in 1992, during the war and prior to the war, in the same block of flats?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, other than the ambulance that you drove, did you drive any other vehicles for the army when you were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the conflict, when Kozarac was attacked, were you in the area where the Muslims were cleared out?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: At the time the conflict broke out in Prijedor municipality, I was in the medical units of the 1st Krajina Corps, exclusively in the medical units and medical teams that went into the field to care for the soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska. In those days, it was still the Territorial Defence, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during that time, you helped only the soldiers who were wounded; is that correct? That was your duty, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rosic, you said -- coming to the event where Mr. Radic called you from the police, did Mr. Radic identify himself when he called? Did he say, "I'm Mladjo Radic"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You answered the phone at the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was the health centre which was at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Radic say as to who was the name of the person who was injured and the person -- the mother's name, the boy's mother's name, to you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: I think he didn't. I don't think he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he -- Mr. Radic, when he called, he said, "I'm Mladjo Radic. I'm calling from the Omarska Police Station." That's your position?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about what Mr. Radic -- how he helped this Denic. You referred to the mother of the boy, the injured boy, as Senada Denic; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rosic, you would have had opportunity to speak with Senada because you said that you were there with her in the first instance when you took the boy and the mother to Banja Luka hospital. Did you know as to who was the husband of this Senada Denic, the name and as to what his profession was?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: She told me that her husband used to work in the Omarska Police Station, though I don't know the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Ibrahim Denic, the policeman who worked in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she tell you as to what happened to Ibrahim Denic during the time of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: I think that she didn't. At that point in time, our only concern, both hers and mine, was the child so we didn't talk about anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct. But later on, because you seem to have taken things from Radic to Mrs. Denic and the boy who was in hospital in Banja Luka, but even that, did you ask as to where her husband was, as to where he was?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Denic stayed in Banja Luka with a woman that we found together --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: -- and I think that she didn't know where her husband was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. My question is: Did she -- I'm asking as to whether she told you at any time about her husband being -- as to where he was during that time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: I think that she told me that she didn't know where he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Radic tell you that Mr. Ibrahim Denic was detained?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- did you ask him as to where this policeman, Mr. Denic, was, ask Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: No. My duties were such that in those days, I didn't have time to talk at any length with anybody. We really were loaded with work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But during these busy times that you talk about, you met Mr. Radic and took things, according to your testimony, to Mrs. Denic when you went to Banja Luka. That's your position; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during this time, didn't you also ask, "Where is the father of this boy?" At least from Mr. Radic, you didn't.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Did Mrs. Denic, Senada Denic, tell you about her brother, Midhat Fazlic who was detained at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: No, she didn't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Radic say that there was a brother of this lady whom he is helping by the name of Midhat Fazlic who was detained at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, did Mr. Radic ask you to assist any other Muslim detainee during this time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: I was mostly assigned to care for soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska. Then everything else was done by the civilian services in those days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't think you understood my question. Did Mr. Radic ask you to assist any other Muslim detainee during this time; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: No. We had no contacts among each other to discuss such things. There were other departments in the health centre who took care of such things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you remember the vehicle JNAK3742, the number?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: I did drive a military ambulance. Whether it had that registration number, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Please bear with me, Your Honour. I have only one more question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question again: Did Mr. Radic ask you to assist any other Muslim during this period?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: I've told you already, my primary responsible was to care for soldiers. Probably they addressed other people in the medical centre who had such responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Waidyaratne. Mr. Jovanovic, any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, just one. Re-examined by Mr. Jovanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, this thing that you did, that you took the child to Banja Luka, was that something outside your regular duties?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Jovanovic. Judge Fouad Riad? Judge Wald? Mr. Rosic, I have a few questions. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Rosic, I have a few questions. If I understood correctly, the health centre where you were working was in Omarska, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And before the conflict, did you work in the same place or not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where were you working before the war?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV ROSIC
utterances.text: In Celpak, a company in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. You've answered my questions. Thank you very much, Mr. Rosic, for coming, and I wish you a safe journey home. The usher will accompany you out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, is the next witness Bogdan Delic? Yes, if we follow the order, then we can anticipate things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Delic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, good morning, Your Honour. I hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will now be reading the solemn declaration handed to you by the usher. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Try and sit comfortably. You will start off by answering questions put to you by Mr. Fila. Mr. Fila, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President, but by your leave, Mr. Zoran Jovanovic has asked to leave the courtroom to call our sixth witness, because I see we're getting things done today quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please go ahead, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, please proceed. Examined by Mr. Fila:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, could you tell us please where and when you were born? I apologise, not Mr. Rosic. Mr. Delic, would you tell us when and where you were born?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1950, on the 15th of April, in Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are you by profession?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: I am a graduate of the political science faculty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you work?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: I work in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your religion?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Marital status?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: I am married with two children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, in 1993, what job were you performing?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: In 1993, I was the Chief of the Public Security Station of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some time during that year, did you propose policeman Mladjo Radic -- did you put him forward for an award of any kind?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were celebrating police day, and his colleagues from the police department of Omarska put him forward for an award, and I passed it on to the authorities for his work merits over a period of 20 years, in addition to a number of other policemen who were put forward for an award as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time in Omarska, it was the police department, was it not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander, the chief?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: The chief of that police department was Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the structure, the makeup and organisation of the police department?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: The police department is the lowest unit numbering 15 to 20 people, and that's how many that particular department had. It had its commander and it had a schedule with shifts. There were patrol leaders, patrol sector leaders. One or two experienced policemen were on the field, on the terrain, who would report back to the commander of the department which was then forwarded on to the police station. And I was informed of the daily occurrences, and if there was any need, then I would react.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that police department -- the police department is where Mladjo Radic worked?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mladjo Radic worked as an ordinary policeman, on the beat, in the Omarska Police Department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what qualifications he held and what he was trained for?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Mladjo Radic, as far as I was informed, worked as an ordinary policeman. He had attended policeman's courses and finished them, graduated, and he had about 20 years of work experience. That was considered a jubilee number of years. On the basis of his work experience, his colleagues put him forward for an award for those 20 years of work. A symbolic sum of money at that time. We did not receive salaries at that time, but it was a sort of remuneration for his 20 years of work and would go towards helping his family to make ends meet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An individual with that kind of qualification, that is to say, who had graduated from a training course, were they in line for any command structure and position of command?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: No. With that kind of qualification, all that people of that kind could be were policemen on the beat, in a sector, covering a certain area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The award that was mentioned, the initiative, as you say, came from the police department, did it not, in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you then passed that nomination on forward. Who did you pass it on to?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: To the Ministry in Banja Luka and the Security Services Centre there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the feedback information you received about the people who were to receive the awards?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: We received a list of people who were to be rewarded for Policeman's Day, the 21st of November. They were symbolic awards. Mladjo would have perhaps got a bigger award, like a gold watch, for his services had the times been normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took the decision to award him?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: The security services sector or, rather, the Ministry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I say that you just signed the decision but you did not bring the decision yourself?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: I could only nominate people for the award but I couldn't make the decision myself, and that is what I did. I passed this nomination on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who compiled the decision itself?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: His colleagues formulated the reasons for which they were nominating him for an award, and I forwarded this. It was his jubilee for working 20 years in the police force, for the kind of conduct he always had, his assistance to younger colleagues, the work he did on the beat, on patrol. He was successful in his work so they compiled a document of this kind by way of nomination. I accepted this and sent it on forward, because Mladjo was, indeed, an experienced policeman. I sent it on to the Banja Luka Security Services Centre and they okayed it, they approved the nomination, along with a list of others, other worthy policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The decision itself, that is to say, the nomination request, was it written in the same way as it was for the other policemen?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. For the years of experience, for the conduct at work and everything else, it would be the same sort of nomination request that was written for everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the award represent a sort of financial contribution in view of the salaries or lack of salaries?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Well, as we did not receive salaries during that time, it was remuneration which would help. We did not receive any salaries in 1992 and 1993, in view of the circumstances and the events that were taking place. And at that time, Mladjo had a large family and so that was another thing that motivated us to help him. In addition to his 20 years of experience, his jubilee of 20 years, we also wished to help the family in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a high-ranking or fairly high-ranking police official, you had occasion to be acquainted with the rules of work of the security organs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were commander, chief of the public security station in Prijedor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, the public security station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any deputies, assistants, department heads, or anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: I had both a deputy and an assistant, and I had police departments which, in turn, had their commanders. We had the traffic police that had its commander; we had the crime squad or crime department. And the police stations also had their chain of command, whereas the police departments did not. They just had the commander for that particular police department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the organisation of the police force, in general terms, generally speaking, is there a service which would be called shift leader?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Well, no. There is only the duty officer or officers who are on standby all the time and at the disposal of the department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, the police department, was it its job to provide security for a building or to step in in the case of a fire or some other extraordinary event?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there were several shifts covering one day, two days, three days, or four days, or whatever, could you tell us how this was organised, how the rotation, the roster was organised and who would do this?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: The department commander knew the exact number of employees, and according to the Rules of Service, he would distribute the workers he had into shifts covering 24 hours. The first shift would work for a certain time and they would be replaced by the second shift, and when they would take over shifts, they would report to the person on duty who would receive the report and then the others would go on duty for the area that was covered, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there were any changes in this schedule, what would happen?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: If there were unforeseen situations like floods or fires, or a traffic accident of any kind, then more policemen would be sent to that area. They would be called, placed on the alert, and go to help out their colleagues for an extraordinary situation of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us return to 1992. You were not in the region of Omarska and Prijedor at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us take the Omarska Police Department, working with a number of policemen and going about its usual business. Suddenly, it receives the task of providing security for the Omarska Investigations Centre. How would it do this? How would it perform that assignment?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Well, the department could not do all this without reinforcements, without having more people sent in as reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm just curious, I don't recall any testimony that this individual was involved in the police department in 1992. That would lead to a lack of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, you will have the opportunity of cross-examining the witness on the subject. The witness said that he wasn't on the spot in Omarska at the time. Mr. Fila went on to ask about the rules and how the rules provided for the situation in Omarska. So you will have your chance, Ms. Somers. But, Mr. Fila, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Providing security for a large centre -- investigation centre of this kind would be much more work, a greater work load.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, it would, and it would mean more people to cover that workload.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you explained to us a moment ago that you would call the reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, the reserve police force or policemen from other departments or sectors, that would be called in as reinforcements and assigned to the various tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the fact that this would be, for example, a provisional security, provide provisional security, temporary security, not permanent but only for a given period of time, what would happen then?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Then a decision would be taken to take on temporary reinforcements, provisional reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. I understand. Would this require a change in the command structure and the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: This would not require a change in the command structure, not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question. Does the commander of a police department, any police department, like the one in Omarska, for example, does he have the right to change command structure?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: No, he does not have the right to change the command structure without agreement from the Ministry or Security Services Centre or the chief of the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To clarify points, a decision would have to be taken at a much higher level; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. A request would have to be sent to me, as the chief of the police station, and I would have to pass it on further up the line to the Public Security Services Centre which would, in turn, have to ask the Ministry of Internal Affairs in order to change the structure work in the area on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to ask you: How long would all this take? If a request came to you and you sent it further up the chain of command, up the line, how long would it take you to receive a decision of this kind back?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: As this is done by telegramme or telegraph, it would require about ten days. If it is an urgent situation, then it might require less than ten days. But usually about ten days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Very well. Would any of the other Defence counsel like to ask the witness any questions? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I have just one question to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead, Mr. Krstan Simic. Cross-examined by Mr. K. Simic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, did you have occasion to learn whether a request of that kind was sent to the Ministry, by the procedure you have just explained?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: During my mandate, we did not because there was no need to. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any of the other counsel? No? I see negative signs. The Prosecution, and it is Ms. Susan Somers, I believe, who is going to cross-examine this witness. Mr. Delic, you will now be answering questions put to you by Ms. Susan Somers. Your witness, Ms. Somers. Cross-examined by Ms. Somers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, in 1992, there was a decision taken by the Crisis Staff, was there not, let's say between May and July, that appointed you to a position of acting principal of the high school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: No, I was not the principal of the primary school but of the high school, the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that's what I asked you. So you were appointed as acting principal of the high school in May 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were an educator; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Professor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An educator. You have never had a day of police training in your life; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, you have not had, or no, you have had. Have you ever had a day of police training in your life?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: No, I have not. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were an active SDS member, were you not? Very active in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You received your appointment to the job succeeding Simo Drljaca because of your political SDS appointment -- I'm sorry, connections, not because of police training; is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: That is not how it was. I was on the battlefield in 1992. In 1993, up till the end -- up to the end of May. And through the media I learned that I was a candidate put forward to perform the function of chief of the police station in Prijedor. It wasn't along political lines. I was not an active member. I was just a member of the League of Communists until 1990; I had been a member for 20 years. And after the end of my political activity within the League of Communists, I voluntarily stepped down from the League of Communists. I was no longer a member, nor was I a member of any other party or appeared as such anywhere. I was probably nominated because I learnt from the newspapers that there were to be some changes, and I learnt that I was probably put forward for my human qualities. I was the principal of secondary schools for ten years; I was a teacher, a professor, for 15 years. Somebody must have remembered my name and put me forward, and that's how I was elected. I took on the job in order to calm the situation. I thought that it would be easier for me doing that rather than being on the battlefield.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What street did you live on in 1991, please? Let's say in June of 1991.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: In 1991, where I live today and where I lived in 1985, and that is Pecani H 36, fourth floor or Petra Zimonjica Mitropolita Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask the usher, for just a moment, to put on an exhibit that I do not intend to seek admission on, just to put it on the ELMO. It is from the Prijedor collection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you a question about it, please. The document is in Serbo-Croat. It is a document, at the top -- excuse me. Could you move it down just a little bit, Mr. Usher? Just a tiny bit. It is dated 24 June, 1991, and it refers to, does it not, members of the municipality of Prijedor in the SDS. Is that your name at the bottom of that list? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I merely wish to draw the Court's attention to the fact that when I did this same thing yesterday with the marriage certificate of the witness, Ms. Susan Somers objected. But as I am chivalrous and a gentleman, I am not going to do that. I am just going to draw the attention of the Court to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, my recollection is that we did not object to it being used in the testimony. We asked questions from it as well. Mr. Fila volunteered to not seek admission until he brought an original, but we had no objection whatsoever to questioning from it. I'm not asking to admit this document. I'd just like to have a question answered from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But would you remind me of yesterday's context? What was the objective of your objection yesterday with respect to the document, the marriage certificate, that was shown, the marriage certificate?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, for interrupting you. I don't recall raising an objection. We asked questions from it. It was at the end of the session yesterday where Mr. Fila made an announcement. I recall no objection whatsoever, to be honest with you. I can check the record that we used the document as well. And he had concerns about its possible validity. We had no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but Mr. Fila will remind us of that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers objected and said that I submitted the document in one copy and that I'm asking the witness questions about a document that the Prosecution has not seen, had a chance to see. Similarly, none of us have seen this document, nor have we been given copies of the document. All I wish to say is that she should not do what she has objected to me doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I had that in mind but I did not want to put that forward. Would it be possible for the Defence to see this document, Ms. Somers? Because we have to clear up a matter. When I say "you," you, both parties, when you're using a document, you should either show it to the other side or not use it. You can use documents and ask questions about them, but could you please show the document to both sides; that is to say, could you now show the document to Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The only copy I have at this time is what is on the ELMO. But if I may let the Court know, there was a 66(B) request and that was the subject of yesterdays discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Somers, but even the Judges would like to see the document at least. So the document can be circulated, if you permit. All we need is to take a look at the document and we'll hand it back to you. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd be very happy to. I'm sorry. We have a technical glitch. Our trial support person is supposed to be bringing down copies for everyone and they have not arrived. So having advanced rather quickly, I do not have extra copies. I would be delighted to give up my copy but that's all I have with me in court now, waiting for the copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I too would like to have a look at the document. Mr. Usher, could you show the Judges the document, please, and the Defence as well. Excuse me. Usher, other counsel, please. Mr. Krstan Simic and then other counsel too. Right. Ms. Susan Somers, you may ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, if you would be kind enough to -- thank you very much. Just a quick question about that document. In June of 1991, did you have any particularly high position in the SDS, or were you simply a member?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: I wasn't a member, nor did I have a high position. I was a principal of a secondary school. Let me just give you an example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: There is a --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to move on. We have very little time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: You can see that this is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to intervene. Ms. Somers, I believe that I heard from the witness that he was a member of the League of Communists and that after that he was not a member of any other party. And you asked him, "Did you have any particularly high position in the SDS?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may be permitted to backtrack and ask if the name Bogdan Delic on this document is a different person from yourself in Prijedor, and is it a very common name?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but this is not my address, because I live in Pecani H 36/4, or at present at Petra Zimonjica. It is my first name and last name, but at that time I was the secondary school principal and I wasn't a member of any party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know any other Bogdan Delics in Prijedor? Do you know any; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you, please, you made a comment -- excuse me. You were asked by Mr. Fila about: "In the organisation of the police force in general terms, generally speaking, is there a service which could be called shift leader?" and your answer was, "No." I'd like to ask a quick question of you. Miroslav Kvocka took the stand recently, and on page -- I'm not sure if it is the official one, but on the 16th of February, Mr. Kvocka made a comment about changes in the police service. He said that Bogdan Delic, who was the chief at that time, "saw for himself that his work was very good. And in the next organisation of the work of the service, there was a decision made whereby I was appointed to the position of the shift leader at the Police Station Prijedor 1." Now, Mr. Kvocka is an experienced police officer. Is there something wrong in his description of that position?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you, if at all, in the Omarska camp? Not the mine before it became the camp, but the camp itself.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you not there as a member of Cigo's group in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you friendly with Radinovic, Momcilo Radinovic, known as Cigo? Have you had any dealings with him politically, professionally?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Political, no, because I wasn't active in politics. But I do know him because Momcilo Radinovic was the municipal mayor in 1992/1993, and we knew each other in 1992 -- 1991/1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your salary when you were a principal for the high school, please? How much money were you making?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Well, it depends. Salaries varied between 1.000 to 2.000 marks, from 200 marks to, depending on the seniority and on the circumstances. At times the salaries were quite sufficient; at times we barely made the ends meet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do after you were working in the Prijedor police structure as the chief of police? What did you do? Did you go off to Serbia for awhile?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you buy some shops and make some money at working some shops?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: I worked privately for my living because my son was studying at the university, and my daughter was in secondary school. And because I was dismissed from work in 1995, I had to begin to work for the public security centre in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not buy a butcher shop and run some other shops in Serbia? Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you decided to give or approve of an award to Mladjo Radic on the -- I guess it's the 11th of August, 1993, that award was because he was such a competent, good policeman, wasn't it? It was for positive contribution to the police force.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how well did you know Radic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew him for about a year. But he was nominated by his colleagues, not by me, his colleagues from Omarska who knew him very well, and his colleagues from the Prijedor Police Station who knew him because Radic used to work in Ljubija. And they suggested to me to forward this nomination to Banja Luka, to the centre, and that is what they did. And the centre accepted it and saw it as a positive move on my side, and that is how it was granted. It also could have ended in a different way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to the interpreters. Did you know what took place at Omarska camp and at Keraterm and at Trnopolje and at Manjaca? Did you know what took place on the territory over which you had police control?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: When I had my term of office with the police, it was quiet and nothing was happening. And before that I was not in the area because I was on the front, and therefore I did not know about that. I know there was a collections centre in Keraterm and Trnopolje and another collection centre in Omarska. What went on and why, I really did not know. I was not there and I had no part in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make it your business to know, or did you ask your predecessor, Simo Drljaca, who closed those camps once their existence and horrors became known to the International Community? Did you ask?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: No, because I wasn't on good terms with Simo. Simo was the one who dismissed me later. We did not discuss that. Simo was in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. "Simo was killed" was the end of the witness' answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- I'm terribly sorry, Your Honour. I was misinformed or I misunderstood something from my own team and I wanted to get a document in but I didn't think I had it. Would the Chamber permit me a minute to show a document that is available to the entire room. I was under the impression that it was still upstairs? No? Okay. I'm sorry. I'm terribly sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Somers, you finished, so -- and I should like to avail myself of this opportunity to tell you, yes, I believe that Mr. Fila had objected because yesterday you objected because the Defence had not given the document to the Prosecution in advance, so that was that. And I think we have to maintain the balance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Fila's people are up reviewing all of our documents now under 66(B) so it's at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. But we know that you have somebody to bring the document in and things can work better. Yes, Mr. Fila, do you have any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour. I don't have any other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Krstan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have only two questions. Further cross-examination by Mr. K. Simic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, in the police system, is there a job called the shift leader? And in your job assignment system, does it say what this person is responsible for?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do these rule also envisage what does a -- what conditions need to be met so that the responsible person in the Ministry appoints a person to that particular workplace?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Judge Riad, do you have any questions? Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You hear me?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Perhaps you are in a position, owing to the important position you were in, to answer my general request. In case of a violation committed by the command, you spoke about the command -- the change of the command structure should be done by the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and so on. In case of a violation committed by one of the commanders, what are the possibilities given to the subordinate people under him to take action or to react?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Well, these possibilities were very limited. A suggestion, proposal, could be made to the higher instance to take appropriate measures against such persons, and how that would be done or not, because one did not necessarily have to believe them. They did not have any direct contact, so that they could do very little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: If they resigned, could they be in danger?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Well, anything may happen. Depends on the circumstances. Criminal charges could be brought against them for the infraction of the Rules of Service. For instance, they could also be brought to account, why they had done this or that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And during the period during which you were in office, did anybody react against anything or resign or make a report concerning a violation, whether in the Omarska camp or anything under your supervision?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Well, I had nothing to do with the Omarska camp at that time so I really don't know. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In general, not necessarily in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: I don't know that anyone resigned. At the time when I was the chief, there was no need for that because the situation was quite satisfactory. It was quiet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you were the chief until 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Between 1993 -- 1993 and 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said that Simo Drljaca dismissed you, I think, in 1995. Was that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Could he dismiss anybody without reason, or was there some kind of motivation?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: He submitted a proposal to the Ministry to dismiss me. Why he did that, I do not know. But be that as it may, I was dismissed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Because you mentioned before that only the Ministry of Internal Affairs was capable of making these changes. So it's the whole -- it seems like a long process which is examined. So did they -- were they -- were you, not accused, but did they take anything against you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I was put on the waiting list on the 15th of May, 1994, and I was on the waiting list until the 2nd of February, 1995, when I received the decision that my contract was terminated in August and that there was no need for it, that I was completely laid off. But I filed charges against them and I won the case, and the judgement was passed in 1996. But I was returned to my job in 1998, only as late as 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you spoke of the award which was given to Mr. Radic, and you mentioned it was for his work in general and his work during 1993. Did this also -- was this also a reward for his attitude, for his work in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: No, it has nothing to do with Omarska. It was for his 20 years of work experience. At the time when I was his chief, his colleagues favourably spoke about his work during those 20 years, and they nominated him and intended it also as a kind of financial assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was he at the Omarska camp at that time, when he got the award?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, I have a few questions and they're all about the award. When you submitted or passed on the proposal from Mr. Radic's colleagues for the award, did you know that he had been a guard at Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not take note of what went on in Omarska camp, and I assume that all the policemen were there to provide security for people who were in the camp in Omarska, because that was the area covered by their police station. So that I assumed that Mladjo Radic was also there as a guard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, when a proposal would come from a police station, or a department, rather, that was in your jurisdiction for you to look at and pass on to the Banja Luka authorities, was any investigation ever made, or did you just look at the fact that colleagues in the policeman's station had proposed him and on that basis alone you might pass it on? Did you do any investigation of your own to see whether this was a person who indeed was good enough and merited the award or had nothing in his background to suggest that he shouldn't get the award? Did you just pass it through, or did you do some looking at the person?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Well, I checked it. Every employee in the police has his file, so I went through the file. And there are also commissions which nominate people for various awards. I also talked to his superior and the commander of the police station in Prijedor and my assistant, and they all had a favourable opinion of him. And on the basis of this, and they agreed and I agreed and we all agreed that I could sign it and forward it to Banja Luka as our nomination. And Mladjo wasn't the only one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Fine. If I understand you correctly, in the course of the checking that you just did, you talked to Mr. Meakic; is that right? Mr. Meakic was then the police chief or commander of the station. Were you aware that he had also been the commander of the camp?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Not of the station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, of the Omarska -- at various times it was departments and station. But whatever it was, you did talk to him and get his approval, as it were, for passing it on. He thought it was a good idea. You checked with him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: The commander of the station department, Meakic, talked to his employees in the department, and they all agreed, after discussion, to nominate Mladjo Radic. And then it reached me -- or, rather, their commander, the police station commander in Prijedor who is responsible for their department, and during this contact and the communication with the commander of the police station in Prijedor, we took over the documentation, the files, went through the files and saw that there were no adverse opinions about Mladjo Radic. And then we decided to forward that nomination to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So, in short, at some point, Mr. Meakic's opinion was sought, too, as his commander.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Do you happen to remember the names of any of the colleague policemen who initiated or supported or whose names were on the proposal for Mr. Radic to get the award?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You don't remember the names of any of the people who actually --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: No. It was not in writing. The proposal was not in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, what was it? Maybe you'll explain it. How did it come to you if it didn't come in writing?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: The document in writing was brought by the commander of the station's department Meakic, and they discussed in their department about whom to nominate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So Meakic came to you and orally told you about the colleagues or the policemen supporting Mr. Radic for this award, right? That's where you got your information from was Mr. Meakic; is that what I understand?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: During the meetings which were held on Mondays, I informed commanders of stations that they should nominate from their departments and stations a certain number of people for awards, for people who had successfully worked for 10 or 20 years. Mladjo Radic had already had 20 years' seniority, and his nomination was discussed in his police department in Omarska, and they decided that they could, indeed, nominate him. I went along with this, and in agreement with the police station in Prijedor, we also considered those nominations and nominations from other departments and other stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. My last question: Did you ever see the -- was the award that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for interrupting you, but I see Ms. Susan Somers on her feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Somers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I apologise for this interruption, but I have to state, in the interests of justice for the Court, the Court is now questioning on a document that I wanted very much to try to get before the Court, even if not admitted, at least identified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I think I understand. I think my own memory suggests to me that in prior testimony before this Court, the subject came up. I would like to just continue with my question as if you hadn't even gotten up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My question for you was: Did you ever see the piece of paper that stated the award that finally went to Mr. Radic? In other words, did you ever see the award, the document, the award document that went to Mr. Radic? Did that ever come to your attention? Whatever they presented him at the time they gave him the 50 Deutschemarks, to your knowledge, did they also present him -- you usually get a document which says you've gotten this award for being so good, et cetera. Did you ever see any document that was his final award?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Those documents were delivered to the police on the police day, on the 21st of November, and they were handed to them personally by the police commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right, fine. Did you ever see the document that was handed to Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: I did not see the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So you don't know what it said on the document as to why he was getting the award.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: We had received a cable from the Minister, from the chief of the centre in Banja Luka. We received a dispatch which said that the nominations are agreed upon and that they would be getting 50 German marks. And there was a list of names in this dispatch, the list of names of people, of men, who had been awarded, the list of persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But you didn't see the actual award certificate. You did not see the actual award certificate that Mr. Radic received; is that right? You don't know what it said on it.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. My last question, then. In the material that you forwarded to the officials in Banja Luka with the proposal for Mr. Radic to receive the awards, there were papers, you told us, that you were forwarded to the Banja Luka authorities who were going to make the final decision; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: In those papers that you forwarded, was there any reference to Mr. Radic's service in the Omarska camp as opposed to his service in the Omarska Police Station? Any reference at all in those papers that you remember and that you forwarded to the Banja Luka authorities?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think it said for his successful work over the past 20 years, that is, between 1976 and 1993, and his participation in providing security for persons and property, and that would cover the Omarska camp because he took part in the guarding of the camp. And I believe he did it very successfully, at least on the basis of what I knew. I do not -- I think he performed his job properly, diligently, as a true professional policeman. I think he discharged all the jobs that were assigned him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me just undergird [sic] this last question, and it's just a yes or no question. In your memory, do you remember, in those papers that were forwarded to Banja Luka, any specific, specific reference to his service in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I mean, I guess that the text also included the security and work in Omarska. I think it said for the successful work in providing security for persons and property and the camp in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Mr. Delic, I have a simple question. You mentioned that there were simply ordinary policemen. Other people also spoke about ordinary policemen, policemen on the beat. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Well, an ordinary policemen is a policemen who performs his tasks and assignments on the ground and is responsible for that; that is, he is in charge of gathering information relative to the security of persons, to protect property and persons, but does not have any other responsibility except to report to his superior about all that he learns on the ground; that is, he performs the simplest, the most ordinary, the commonest tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the expression "ordinary," "common policeman," is there a difference between an ordinary and a common policeman?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Well, we're all responsible policemen. We're all responsible policemen. If we perform our jobs responsibly, if we are covering the ground, then an ordinary policeman must report about that, must submit his accounts. Everybody has to do that. But he is not the superior. He cannot take any decisions without his superiors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question. This wording, ordinary policeman, common policeman, do you find it in the rules? Is that an officer, a law enforcement officer? What kind of officer is that? Is it in the rules?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Well, no, you won't find the word "ordinary" or "common"; you will find the word "policeman." But by this we mean because if there is a policeman with specific responsibilities and a policeman who can be a superior and a policeman who is not a superior. A common policeman is not an officer. He cannot issue an order; that is, he may order citizens to remove something or whatever, but he cannot issue orders to other policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. If I understand you well, this word "ordinary policeman," that is not an official term, and the police use this word in order to make a distinction between different levels of responsibility within the police force itself; is that it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Very well, very well. Thank you very much. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, excuse me, Mr. Simic, I believe that Judge Riad has another question, but we shall then adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, in your answer to my colleague Judge Wald, you mentioned that the award also included the successful work in Omarska. First, did other people working in Omarska receive an award to your knowledge, or was Mr. Radic the only one who got an award?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: No, Radic was not awarded for Omarska, let us make that quite clear. Radic was awarded for 20 years for successful work, between 1972 and 1993, and that was the first time that we marked the police day, the 21st of November. He was the man with the longer service in the police work there, and therefore he was awarded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just wanted to know what you meant by successful work in Omarska. What did you mean by successful work in Omarska, as a concentration [Realtime transcript read in error "camp"] camp?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: I was not in Omarska at the time, and I was not a superior there at the time, but I assumed that all the policemen from the Omarska department took part in the security duties in Omarska, the protection of people. And from what I know, they did it all very correctly and professionally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Delic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, excuse me, what is it that you want in the first place? What is it that you want? Why are you on your feet? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] His Honour, Judge Riad, asked the witness a question related to the consequences about the dismissal of the police at the time, and I wanted to ask a question of the witness in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. There is just a word missing in the transcript. I asked, "What did you mean by successful work in Omarska as a concentration camp," and they didn't write the word "concentration." I want it to be added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, I think there were several interruptions, and I believe that some discipline in our work would be in order. Mr. Simic was speaking. So, Mr. Simic, you will complete what you had to say. I understood that there was a question derived from Judge Riad's question, but we have to finish, but do ask your question. Further cross-examination by Mr. K. Simic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, under the conditions of a war, had a policeman under any rank, if he was militarily able, could the police submit his resignation, or could he have been thrown out of the police? What could have happened to him?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN DELIC
utterances.text: Well, it is more than likely that he would have been sent to the front line, and criminal charges would have been filed against such policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, did you also want to ask an additional question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It would have gone back, Your Honour, to a question raised by Her Honour Judge Wald, if I'm permitted. If not -- no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Ms. Somers, I was asking you if you have any question that derives from Mr. Simic's question. Is that how I understand it, that you do not have a question that derives from Mr. Simic's question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Ms. Somers -- we've agreed with Ms. Somers not to use the word "concentration camp" because the order issued when the Omarska camp was set up was the investigation camp, and I do not know how Judge Riad can insist that it was a concentration camp. I believe that you will decide on this in your judgement. But at any rate, this is untimely to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, Mr. Fila. We are not deciding now yes or no. That is what you said, and the transcript speaks for itself. Ms. Somers, what was your question which derived from the Judge's question? I believe you said that you might have a question which would be a follow-up on a question asked by Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would require identifying a document and just making sure that the particular theme of conversation that was the subject of Judge Wald's questions is the same document I'm looking to. Just document identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then perhaps the usher could show it to us, and Judge Wald could see the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This document has been provided to the Defence much earlier, and this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, will you please ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the Defence does wish an extra copy for now, there is no problem. We have ... Mr. Usher, if I may ask you to distribute -- we have extra copies for the Defence, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, I ask you only to show the document to Judge Wald. This is not now the time to distribute the document to other parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We always want to benefit from something, something that was not said that it will be done. So therefore --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour. My fault entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me just clarify. I simply asked the witness questions about what he remembered was in the document, which he answered on the spot. True, many months ago, we had some testimony about a document like this, but I did not have it in front of me so I was not referring to a specific document that I could identify at the time. I was asking him cold a question about what was in the document, which he answered. So I don't think it's particularly relevant to identify a particular document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: All right. Then I should -- that's fine. My question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, Ms. Somers, we shall now return the document, and that will be the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'll leave it for later. I'll just hang onto it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall -- this testimony is now over. Mr. Delic, we have no further questions for you. Thank you very much for coming here. I wish you a happy return to your home and your place of work. Thank you. The usher will help you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall now adjourn for 50 minutes. I believe we all need a break. Fifty minutes. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.10 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before I call the next witness, allow me to make a point. A small problem has arisen linked to the translation and differences in languages. The interpreters have drawn my attention to this, and I think that the Prosecution has been informed, as have Your Honours. At one point, I asked the previous witness, Mr. Delic, whether there was razvodnik straze or guard shift leader in the police. It is a military term. It is a person who takes the guards from one position to another. That applies to the military. And the question was whether such a position existed in the police. His answer was no. However, in the English transcript, his answer appeared to be that there were no shift leaders in the police, which is not my question nor was it his answer. So as not to call in question the credibility of the witness, and as far as I know in a similar case, I think it was the Celebici trial, the tape was reviewed, the audiotape, and then it was established what exactly was asked and what the exact answer was. So I should like to appeal to you that something similar be done in this case; otherwise, we have three different answers. Because, as you know, I'm listening to the French interpretation, and there the interpretation was different again. So thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that particular term that was used in B/C/S has been the subject of discussion with the head of the -- the English B/C/S translation services, Mrs. Tina Zoric, and in fact the determination by Translation Services is that in the context of discussions involving Radic, because that's where it came up, that the correct translation is "shift leader." The use of military terms have been, for one reason or another, interjected into the vocabulary, but they have made their own philological, linguistic determination that that is correct. And if the Chamber would wish to have Mrs. Zoric address it about that, I can only relate what has already come up because we have discussed this in connection with another document. I informed the individual from Translation Services who approached me and asked her also to confirm this with Mrs. Zoric, and I'm sure Mrs. Zoric would be happy to explain it to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
